gloss_terse: Mouth; by extension: edge of sword, opening, command, proportion, end, portion, collar of garment
gloss_readable: One of the most versatile nouns in Biblical Hebrew, peh fundamentally denotes the mouth as the organ of speech and eating. From this concrete anchor the word radiates outward: the 'mouth' of a sword becomes its killing edge, the 'mouth' of a well its opening, and the 'mouth' of a king his authoritative command. In proportional idioms (al-pi, lefi) it means 'according to' or 'in measure with.' The same spatial logic yields 'end, extremity' of a place, 'portion' of an inheritance, and even the collar-opening of a priestly garment. Cross-linguistically, Spanish boca, French bouche, and German Mund track the literal sense, while the idiomatic extensions diverge revealingly across target languages.

senses.1: The physical mouth of a person or animal, overwhelmingly the most frequent use at 395 occurrences. Spanish boca-de and French bouche-de mirror the Hebrew construct-chain pattern faithfully. Appears from Genesis 29 (the well's mouth doubles as sense 4) through the Psalms and Prophets wherever literal speech or eating is in view.
senses.2: The sharpened edge of a sword, almost always in the idiom lefi-cherev ('by the mouth/edge of the sword'). At 47 occurrences this is a well-established dead metaphor. Spanish a-filo-de and French avec-tranchant-de both abandon the 'mouth' image for 'blade/edge,' while German durch-Mund-von preserves it. Genesis 34:26 and Joshua's conquest narratives are the heartland passages.
senses.3: A prepositional idiom meaning 'according to, in proportion to, as befits,' formed with al-pi or lefi. Spanish segun and French selon translate the sense without any bodily reference, confirming full grammaticalization. Exodus 12:4 (Passover lamb portioned al-pi) and Exodus 16:16-21 (manna measured lefi) are classic instances.
senses.4: The opening or entrance of a physical container: a well, sack, cave, or the neck-hole of a garment (overlapping with sense 8). At 12 occurrences, Spanish abertura-de and French ouverture-de show the shift from 'mouth' to 'opening.' Exodus 28:32 prescribes the pi of the priestly robe, and Genesis 29:2-3 describes the stone over the pi of the well.
senses.5: A metonymic extension where 'mouth' stands for the authoritative word, command, or decree that issues from it. German Befehl ('command') appears alongside Mund ('mouth'), exposing the metaphor. Genesis 45:21 ('at the mouth of Pharaoh') and Proverbs 8:29 ('when he set a decree for the sea') illustrate the range from royal to divine authority.
senses.6: The far end or extremity of a spatial extent, attested four times. In 2 Kings 10:21 the temple was full 'mouth to mouth' (end to end) and in 2 Kings 21:16 Jerusalem was filled with blood 'mouth to mouth.' Spanish extremo and French a-bouche reveal how some languages re-lexicalize while others retain the body metaphor.
senses.7: A measured share or proportional portion, as in the 'double mouth' (pi shenayim) of the firstborn's inheritance (Deut 21:17) and Elisha's request for a double portion of Elijah's spirit (2 Kgs 2:9). Spanish porcion-de and French part-de confirm the semantic shift from 'mouth' to 'portion.' Zechariah 13:8 divides the land into three 'mouths.'
senses.8: The collar or neck opening of a robe through which the head passes, attested in Job 30:18 and Psalm 133:2. Spanish cuello-de ('collar of') and German wie-Mund-von ('like-mouth-of') show the split between languages that re-lexicalize and those that calque. Closely related to sense 4 but specialized to garments.
senses.9: A hapax use in 1 Samuel 13:21 where pim appears as a unit of weight or price (approximately two-thirds of a shekel) for sharpening agricultural tools. All target languages simply transliterate pim, and archaeological pim-weights confirm this as a technical term unrelated to the 'mouth' semantic field.

gloss_terse: To go down, descend; Hifil: bring down, send down; Hofal: be brought down; of liquids: flow down; of structures: collapse
gloss_readable: A primary verb of downward motion, yarad is the natural counterpart of alah ('go up'). In the Qal it describes physical descent from mountains, into valleys, or down to Egypt and Sheol. The Hifil causative extends the range to bringing down persons, lowering objects, and God sending down rain or judgment. Poetically, tears 'go down' the face (Lam 3:48) and anointing oil 'runs down' Aaron's beard (Ps 133:2). The participial formula yorde bor ('those going down to the pit') becomes a standing epithet for the dead. Across languages, Spanish bajar, French descendre, and German hinabgehen consistently mark the core downward vector.

senses.1: The primary Qal sense of physical downward movement, accounting for 242 of 381 occurrences. Persons descend from hills, go down to Egypt, enter cities at lower elevation. Spanish bajar/descendio and French descendit track faithfully. Genesis 12:10 (Abram going down to Egypt) and Exodus 19:14,20 (Moses descending Sinai) are paradigmatic.
senses.2: The Hifil causative: to bring down, take down, or lead down persons or objects. At 53 occurrences it is the most common derived stem. Spanish hizo-descender and French apporte-en-bas preserve the causative structure. Genesis 37:25 (Joseph brought down to Egypt) and Genesis 42:38 (Jacob refusing to send Benjamin down) anchor the patriarchal narratives.
senses.3: The Qal active participle used as a substantive, especially in the formula yorde bor/sheol ('those going down to the pit/Sheol'). This 44-occurrence cluster appears across Ezekiel 26-32 and the Psalms. Spanish los-que-descienden and French descendre capture the participial nominalization. Genesis 28:12 (angels descending the ladder) is the earliest instance.
senses.4: Yarad applied to liquids flowing or running downward: tears streaming down a face, rain descending, oil running down Aaron's beard. Spanish derrama ('pours') and French descendre maintain the vertical image. Psalm 133:2 and Lamentations 3:48 are the most vivid poetic uses, with 15 total occurrences.
senses.5: The Hifil used figuratively for divine or authoritative action: sending down rain, fire, or judgment, and humbling the proud. At 13 occurrences this extends beyond physical causation into theological territory. German brings-hinab and French apporter-en-bas reveal the metaphorical stretch. 1 Samuel 2:6 ('YHWH brings down to Sheol') and Psalm 56:7 are key passages.
senses.6: The Hofal passive: to be brought down or made to descend, attested 6 times. Spanish fue-bajado and French etait-pris-en-bas mark the passive voice clearly. Isaiah 14:11,15 (the king of Babylon brought down to Sheol) and Ezekiel 31:18 provide the most dramatic instances of forced humiliation.
senses.7: The Qal infinitive construct with prepositions functioning as a temporal clause or verbal noun: 'when he came down,' 'its going down,' 'from descending.' Four occurrences show this grammaticalized use. Exodus 34:29 (Moses' face shining be-ridto, 'when he came down') is the most theologically significant instance.
senses.8: Yarad used of structures collapsing or falling down, attested three times. Walls and fortifications 'come down' under siege. Spanish caida ('fall') and German fallen depart from the standard descent vocabulary, revealing that this sense borders on a distinct lexeme. Deuteronomy 20:20 and Isaiah 32:19 provide the clearest examples.
senses.9: A single anomalous occurrence in 2 Samuel 18:4 where the expected 'went down' appears as 'went out' across all target languages (English went-out, Spanish salieron, French alla-dehors). This likely reflects a textual or contextual peculiarity where yarad is used for exiting a gate or passage, blending descent with departure.

gloss_terse: To sin, miss the mark; Hifil: cause to sin; Piel: purify from sin; Hitpael: purify oneself; also: sinner, bear loss
gloss_readable: At its etymological root, chata means to miss a target or go astray from a path, and this concrete image underlies all its moral and ritual extensions. In the Qal it overwhelmingly denotes sinning against God or moral law, as confessed from Pharaoh (Exod 9:27) to David (2 Sam 12:13). The Hifil causative indicts those who lead others into sin, notably Jeroboam's recurring epithet. Remarkably, the Piel and Hitpael reverse the direction entirely: rather than committing sin, they denote purifying from sin and undergoing purification, reflecting the priestly ritual system. The Arabic cognate khatia preserves both the 'err/miss' and 'sin' meanings, while Korean choe-reul jitda and Swahili -tenda dhambi capture only the moral sense.

senses.1: The core Qal sense of committing sin or transgression, dominating with 165 occurrences. Spanish he-pecado and French ai-je-pecha mirror the confessional formula 'I have sinned.' Leviticus 4 builds the entire sin-offering system around this verb, and 1 Kings repeatedly uses it for royal apostasy. Arabic khatia preserves both 'err' and 'sin' nuances.
senses.2: The Hifil causative: to cause or lead another to sin. At 32 occurrences this is almost a technical term for Jeroboam's legacy in Kings, where he 'caused Israel to sin' (1 Kgs 14:16 and passim). Spanish hizo-pecar and French causa-a-peche neatly render the causative. Deuteronomy 24:4 warns against causing the land to sin through remarriage violations.
senses.3: The Piel factitive/denominative meaning to purify from sin or perform a sin offering, inverting the root's usual moral direction into ritual restoration. Fourteen occurrences cluster in Leviticus and Numbers. Spanish purificara and French purifia confirm the semantic reversal. Exodus 29:36 (purifying the altar) and Leviticus 14:49 (purifying a house from disease) are foundational.
senses.4: The Hitpael reflexive: to purify oneself or undergo ritual purification, attested 9 times. Numbers 19:12-20 is the primary locus, specifying purification after corpse contamination. Spanish se-purificaron and French purifia-eux-memes capture the reflexive action. This sense complements the Piel by making the subject both agent and patient of cleansing.
senses.5: The Qal participle used as a substantive noun meaning 'sinner, one who sins,' a fixed category of moral identity rather than a momentary act. Nine occurrences appear mainly in Wisdom literature. Spanish pecador and French pecher (used nominally) correspond to Arabic al-khati. Ecclesiastes 2:26 and Proverbs 13:22 contrast the sinner with the righteous as opposing archetypes.
senses.6: The Qal participle functioning verbally to describe ongoing sinning rather than naming a person as a sinner. Eight occurrences in prophetic and wisdom contexts. Spanish peca ('sins' as active verb) and French pechant ('sinning') mark the verbal force. Isaiah 1:4 ('a sinning nation') and Proverbs 14:21 illustrate the attributive and predicative uses.
senses.7: A hapax in Judges 20:16 preserving the original concrete meaning: to miss a target. Seven hundred Benjamite slingers could hurl stones at a hair and 'not miss.' All target languages render this as 'miss' rather than 'sin,' and Arabic khatia retains both senses, confirming the etymological bridge between missing a mark and moral failure.
senses.8: A hapax in Genesis 31:39 where Jacob tells Laban he personally bore the loss of any stolen animal. English bore-loss-of-it and German musste-es-bussen ('had to pay for it') point toward a commercial or liability sense: to bear the penalty or absorb the cost. This bridges the moral and financial dimensions of the root.
senses.9: A hapax in Isaiah 29:21 in a Hifil participial construction: 'those who make a man an offender by a word.' Spanish los-que-hacen-pecar ('those who cause to sin') aligns this with sense 2's causative, but the forensic context of false accusation in a legal setting gives it a distinct juridical coloring not present in the Jeroboam formula.

gloss_terse: To take possession of, inherit; Hifil: dispossess, drive out, or grant as inheritance; Nifal: become poor
gloss_readable: Few Hebrew verbs carry as much covenantal weight as yarash. In the Qal it spans from taking possession of the promised land (the dominant usage in Deuteronomy and Joshua) to inheriting property within a family line. The Hifil causative splits dramatically: it can mean either to dispossess the current inhabitants or to grant someone an inheritance, depending on context. Most strikingly, the Nifal reflexive means to become poor or impoverished, as if being 'dispossessed' of one's own wealth. The Arabic cognate waritha ('inherit') and the Ethiopic warada confirm the ancient inheritance semantics, while the dispossession and impoverishment senses appear to be inner-Hebrew developments tied to conquest theology.

senses.1: The primary Qal sense: to take possession of land, especially the promised land in covenant contexts. At 130 occurrences this dominates Deuteronomy and Joshua. Spanish poseerla and French posseder-cela mirror the possessive semantics. Deuteronomy 2:31 and 4:5 use the idiom bo-resheth ('enter to possess') as the standard formula for the conquest mandate.
senses.2: The Hifil causative meaning to dispossess or drive out inhabitants, the violent counterpart to sense 1's settlement. Sixty-one occurrences concentrate in Numbers 33 and Deuteronomy. Spanish desposeyo and French deposseda capture the privative force. Numbers 33:52-53 pairs the command to dispossess (Hifil) with the command to possess (Qal), showing the two senses as sequential phases of conquest.
senses.3: The Qal sense of inheriting as an heir within family succession or covenant promise, attested 18 times. Arabic yarithu and Swahili -rithi preserve this precise cognate meaning. Genesis 15:3-8 is the foundational passage where Abraham asks who will 'inherit' him, and God promises the land as a possession. Distinct from sense 1 in emphasizing legal succession rather than military occupation.
senses.4: The Qal participle used substantivally to mean 'heir, possessor, one who inherits,' with 9 occurrences. Arabic warith and Korean sangsokja ('inheritor') correspond precisely. Genesis 15:3 introduces the term when Abraham laments that his household servant is his yoresh ('heir'). Numbers 36:8 and 2 Samuel 14:7 use it in legal inheritance disputes.
senses.5: The Qal used with personal objects to mean dispossessing persons from their territory, distinct from the Hifil's causative grammar. Four occurrences in Deuteronomy 2:12-22 describe successive waves of peoples dispossessing one another. Spanish despojaron and French deposseda-eux confirm the hostile sense. Judges 14:15 extends this to a domestic threat context.
senses.6: The Hifil used as a positive causative: to cause someone to inherit, to grant as a possession or bequeath. Four occurrences represent the semantic mirror of sense 2's dispossession. Spanish diste-en-posesion ('gave in possession') and French causes-tu-a-posseder capture the benefactive meaning. Judges 11:24 and Ezra 9:12 are key texts.
senses.7: The Nifal meaning to become poor or impoverished, a remarkable semantic development from 'possess' to 'be dispossessed of one's wealth.' Four occurrences in Proverbs and Genesis. Spanish empobrecian and Swahili kuwa-maskini ('become destitute') confirm the poverty reading. Proverbs 20:13 warns the lazy will become poor, and Genesis 45:11 has Joseph rescuing his family lest they be impoverished.
senses.8: A hapax in 1 Samuel 2:7 where God 'impoverishes' (Hifil or Polel), forming a pair with 'enriches.' English impoverishes and Spanish empobrece render the active causative of poverty. This bridges senses 2 and 7: God both dispossesses and impoverishes as sovereign acts, linking the military and economic dimensions of the root.
senses.9: A hapax in Deuteronomy 28:42 where locusts 'possess' or take over the trees and produce of the land. English possesses and Spanish poseera apply yarash to insect infestation as a grim covenant-curse reversal: the land Israel was commanded to yarash is itself yarash-ed by destructive creatures, a deliberate irony in the curse catalog.
